CHAPTER XVII.


Mrs. Dashwood was surprised only for a moment at seeing him; for his
coming to Barton was, in her opinion, of all things the most natural.
Her joy and expression of regard long outlived her wonder. He received
the kindest welcome from her; and shyness, coldness, reserve could not
stand against such a reception. They had begun to fail him before he
entered the house, and they were quite overcome by the captivating
manners of Mrs. Dashwood. Indeed a man could not very well be in love
with either of her daughters, without extending the passion to her; and
Elinor had the satisfaction of seeing him soon become more like
himself. His affections seemed to reanimate towards them all, and his
interest in their welfare again became perceptible. He was not in
spirits, however; he praised their house, admired its prospect, was
attentive, and kind; but still he was not in spirits. The whole family
perceived it, and Mrs. Dashwood, attributing it to some want of
liberality in his mother, sat down to table indignant against all
selfish parents.

“What are Mrs. Ferrars’s views for you at present, Edward?” said she,
when dinner was over and they had drawn round the fire; “are you still
to be a great orator in spite of yourself?”

“No. I hope my mother is now convinced that I have no more talents than
inclination for a public life!”

“But how is your fame to be established? for famous you must be to
satisfy all your family; and with no inclination for expense, no
affection for strangers, no profession, and no assurance, you may find
it a difficult matter.”

“I shall not attempt it. I have no wish to be distinguished; and have
every reason to hope I never shall. Thank Heaven! I cannot be forced
into genius and eloquence.”

“You have no ambition, I well know. Your wishes are all moderate.”

“As moderate as those of the rest of the world, I believe. I wish as
well as every body else to be perfectly happy; but, like every body
else it must be in my own way. Greatness will not make me so.”

“Strange that it would!” cried Marianne. “What have wealth or grandeur
to do with happiness?”

“Grandeur has but little,” said Elinor, “but wealth has much to do with
it.”

“Elinor, for shame!” said Marianne, “money can only give happiness
where there is nothing else to give it. Beyond a competence, it can
afford no real satisfaction, as far as mere self is concerned.”

“Perhaps,” said Elinor, smiling, “we may come to the same point. _Your_
competence and _my_ wealth are very much alike, I dare say; and without
them, as the world goes now, we shall both agree that every kind of
external comfort must be wanting. Your ideas are only more noble than
mine. Come, what is your competence?”

“About eighteen hundred or two thousand a year; not more than _that_.”

Elinor laughed. “_two_ thousand a year! _one_ is my wealth! I guessed
how it would end.”

“And yet two thousand a-year is a very moderate income,” said Marianne.
“A family cannot well be maintained on a smaller. I am sure I am not
extravagant in my demands. A proper establishment of servants, a
carriage, perhaps two, and hunters, cannot be supported on less.”

Elinor smiled again, to hear her sister describing so accurately their
future expenses at Combe Magna.

“Hunters!” repeated Edward—“but why must you have hunters? Every body
does not hunt.”

Marianne coloured as she replied, “But most people do.”

“I wish,” said Margaret, striking out a novel thought, “that somebody
would give us all a large fortune apiece!”

“Oh that they would!” cried Marianne, her eyes sparkling with
animation, and her cheeks glowing with the delight of such imaginary
happiness.

“We are all unanimous in that wish, I suppose,” said Elinor, “in spite
of the insufficiency of wealth.”

“Oh dear!” cried Margaret, “how happy I should be! I wonder what I
should do with it!”

Marianne looked as if she had no doubt on that point.

“I should be puzzled to spend so large a fortune myself,” said Mrs.
Dashwood, “if my children were all to be rich without my help.”

“You must begin your improvements on this house,” observed Elinor, “and
your difficulties will soon vanish.”

“What magnificent orders would travel from this family to London,” said
Edward, “in such an event! What a happy day for booksellers,
music-sellers, and print-shops! You, Miss Dashwood, would give a
general commission for every new print of merit to be sent you—and as
for Marianne, I know her greatness of soul, there would not be music
enough in London to content her. And books!—Thomson, Cowper, Scott—she
would buy them all over and over again: she would buy up every copy, I
believe, to prevent their falling into unworthy hands; and she would
have every book that tells her how to admire an old twisted tree.
Should not you, Marianne? Forgive me, if I am very saucy. But I was
willing to show you that I had not forgot our old disputes.”

“I love to be reminded of the past, Edward—whether it be melancholy or
gay, I love to recall it—and you will never offend me by talking of
former times. You are very right in supposing how my money would be
spent—some of it, at least—my loose cash would certainly be employed in
improving my collection of music and books.”

“And the bulk of your fortune would be laid out in annuities on the
authors or their heirs.”

“No, Edward, I should have something else to do with it.”

“Perhaps, then, you would bestow it as a reward on that person who
wrote the ablest defence of your favourite maxim, that no one can ever
be in love more than once in their life—your opinion on that point is
unchanged, I presume?”

“Undoubtedly. At my time of life opinions are tolerably fixed. It is
not likely that I should now see or hear any thing to change them.”

“Marianne is as steadfast as ever, you see,” said Elinor, “she is not
at all altered.”

“She is only grown a little more grave than she was.”

“Nay, Edward,” said Marianne, “_you_ need not reproach me. You are not
very gay yourself.”

“Why should you think so!” replied he, with a sigh. “But gaiety never
was a part of _my_ character.”

“Nor do I think it a part of Marianne’s,” said Elinor; “I should hardly
call her a lively girl—she is very earnest, very eager in all she
does—sometimes talks a great deal and always with animation—but she is
not often really merry.”

“I believe you are right,” he replied, “and yet I have always set her
down as a lively girl.”

“I have frequently detected myself in such kind of mistakes,” said
Elinor, “in a total misapprehension of character in some point or
other: fancying people so much more gay or grave, or ingenious or
stupid than they really are, and I can hardly tell why or in what the
deception originated. Sometimes one is guided by what they say of
themselves, and very frequently by what other people say of them,
without giving oneself time to deliberate and judge.”

“But I thought it was right, Elinor,” said Marianne, “to be guided
wholly by the opinion of other people. I thought our judgments were
given us merely to be subservient to those of neighbours. This has
always been your doctrine, I am sure.”

“No, Marianne, never. My doctrine has never aimed at the subjection of
the understanding. All I have ever attempted to influence has been the
behaviour. You must not confound my meaning. I am guilty, I confess, of
having often wished you to treat our acquaintance in general with
greater attention; but when have I advised you to adopt their
sentiments or to conform to their judgment in serious matters?”

“You have not been able to bring your sister over to your plan of
general civility,” said Edward to Elinor, “Do you gain no ground?”

“Quite the contrary,” replied Elinor, looking expressively at Marianne.

“My judgment,” he returned, “is all on your side of the question; but I
am afraid my practice is much more on your sister’s. I never wish to
offend, but I am so foolishly shy, that I often seem negligent, when I
am only kept back by my natural awkwardness. I have frequently thought
that I must have been intended by nature to be fond of low company, I
am so little at my ease among strangers of gentility!”

“Marianne has not shyness to excuse any inattention of hers,” said
Elinor.

“She knows her own worth too well for false shame,” replied Edward.
“Shyness is only the effect of a sense of inferiority in some way or
other. If I could persuade myself that my manners were perfectly easy
and graceful, I should not be shy.”

“But you would still be reserved,” said Marianne, “and that is worse.”

Edward started—“Reserved! Am I reserved, Marianne?”

“Yes, very.”

“I do not understand you,” replied he, colouring. “Reserved!—how, in
what manner? What am I to tell you? What can you suppose?”

Elinor looked surprised at his emotion; but trying to laugh off the
subject, she said to him, “Do not you know my sister well enough to
understand what she means? Do not you know she calls every one reserved
who does not talk as fast, and admire what she admires as rapturously
as herself?”

Edward made no answer. His gravity and thoughtfulness returned on him
in their fullest extent—and he sat for some time silent and dull.

Mrs. Dashwood’s surprise at his arrival lasted only a moment—for his coming to Barton seemed, to her, the most natural thing in the world. Her warmth and kindness far outshone any lingering astonishment, and he was met with such genuine affection that any trace of hesitation in him could not withstand it. Indeed, before he had even crossed the threshold, his reserve had begun to soften, and under Mrs. Dashwood’s gracious welcome, it melted entirely.

It was impossible, after all, for a man to love either of her daughters without extending some measure of that devotion to their mother as well. Elinor, observing him closely, was pleased to see him gradually ease into his usual manner, his attentions reawakening, his concern for their well-being becoming evident once more. Yet despite this, his spirits were undeniably low. He complimented their home, admired the view, and was as courteous as ever—but the shadow over him was unmistakable.

The entire family noticed, and Mrs. Dashwood, quick to lay the blame upon his mother’s supposed miserliness, took her seat at dinner with fresh indignation toward all parents who put their own interests before their children’s happiness.

Once they had gathered by the fire after the meal, she turned to him with directness.

“And what plans has Mrs. Ferrars laid out for you now, Edward? Are you still to be thrust into greatness against your will?”

“No,” he replied. “I believe my mother is at last convinced that I possess neither the talent nor the inclination for public life.”

“But how, then, will you achieve the renown your family expects? For famous you must be, and yet you shun expense, avoid strangers, have no profession, and lack the boldness to impose yourself upon the world. It strikes me as a difficult path.”

“I do not intend to attempt it. I have no desire for distinction—and every reason to hope I shall never attain it. Heaven be thanked, I cannot be forced into eloquence or genius.”

“Ambition was never your failing,” Mrs. Dashwood remarked. “Your wishes have always been modest.”

“As modest as any man’s, I suppose. Like everyone else, I wish to be happy—but, like everyone else, it must be on my own terms. Greatness would not secure it for me.”

“How strange that it should!” Marianne exclaimed. “What has wealth or grandeur to do with happiness?”

“Grandeur, very little,” Elinor said mildly. “But wealth has rather more to do with it.”

Marianne turned to her sister with playful reproach. “Elinor, for shame! Money can only bring happiness where nothing else does. Beyond a comfortable living, it offers no true satisfaction—not in matters of the heart.”

Elinor smiled. “Perhaps we are not so far apart as you think. *Your* idea of comfort and *mine* may well be the same. Without it, as the world stands, we must both agree that life would lack ease. You only phrase it more nobly. Come, then—what is this competence you speak of?”

“Perhaps eighteen hundred or two thousand a year. No more than that.”

Elinor laughed. “Two thousand! And *one* is my idea of wealth! I see how this will end.”

“And yet two thousand a year is hardly excessive,” Marianne countered. “A family cannot live decently on less. I assure you, I am not unreasonable—a proper household staff, a carriage, perhaps two, and hunters cannot be kept on a smaller income.”

Elinor’s smile deepened at her sister’s precise accounting of their imagined expenses at Combe Magna.

“Hunters?” Edward repeated. “But why must you have hunters? Not everyone hunts.”

Marianne flushed slightly. “Most people do.”

Margaret, struck by a sudden thought, interjected, “I wish someone would give each of us a vast fortune!”

“Oh, if only they would!” Marianne cried, her eyes alight at the fantasy.

“I suppose we are all in agreement on that,” Elinor said dryly, “despite our differing views on the necessity of wealth.”

Margaret sighed dreamily. “How happy I should be! I wonder what I would do with it all!”

Marianne’s expression suggested she had no such uncertainty.

Mrs. Dashwood chuckled. “I confess, I should be at a loss myself—if my children were all rich without my help.”

“You might begin by improving this house,” Elinor suggested. “That would solve the dilemma quickly enough.”

Edward smiled faintly. “What a flurry of orders would go up to London from this household! The booksellers, the music shops—they would rejoice. You, Miss Dashwood, would demand every new print of merit, and Marianne—” He glanced at her. “Well, I know her soul. There would not be enough music in all of London to satisfy her. And books! Thomson, Cowper, Scott—she would buy them all, again and again, if only to keep them from lesser hands. She would own every volume that teaches one to admire a gnarled old tree. Am I wrong, Marianne? Forgive me if I presume too much—but I wished to prove I have not forgotten our old debates.”

Marianne’s face softened. “I love to remember the past, Edward—whether sweet or sorrowful. You could never offend me by speaking of it. And you are quite right in guessing how I would spend my fortune—or at least part of it. My ready money would certainly go to music and books.”

“And the rest?” he teased. “Annuities for the authors, perhaps?”

“No,” she said with a quiet smile. “I should find other uses for it.”

“Ah, then perhaps a reward for whoever best defends your favorite belief—that one can only truly love once in a lifetime? Unless your opinion has changed?”

“It has not. At my age, opinions are rather fixed. I doubt anything could alter them now.”

“You see, Edward,” Elinor said lightly, “Marianne is as steadfast as ever. She has not changed at all.”

“Only grown a little more serious,” he observed.

Marianne met his gaze. “You need not reproach me, Edward. You are hardly in spirits yourself.”

He sighed. “Gaiety was never part of my nature.”

“Nor hers,” Elinor added. “I would not call Marianne a *lively* girl—she is earnest, eager in all she does, often speaks with passion—but she is not often truly merry.”

Edward nodded slowly. “I suppose you are right—though I always thought of her as lively.”

“I have often made such mistakes,” Elinor mused. “Misjudging someone as more cheerful or solemn than they truly are. Sometimes we are swayed by what people say of themselves—or more often, by what others say of them—without pausing to form our own judgment.”

Marianne raised a brow. “But I thought it was proper to be guided by others’ opinions. I believed our own judgments were meant only to serve those of our neighbors. Surely that has always been your doctrine?”

Elinor laughed. “No, indeed! I have never argued for the surrender of one’s own understanding. I only wished to guide *behavior*—not thought. You must not mistake me. I may have urged you to show more courtesy in company, but when have I ever advised you to adopt their sentiments on matters of importance?”

Edward turned to Elinor with amusement. “You have not succeeded in converting your sister to your philosophy of general politeness, then? No progress?”

“Quite the opposite,” Elinor said, casting a meaningful glance at Marianne.

“My judgment is entirely on your side,” Edward admitted. “But my actions, I fear, align more with Marianne’s. I never mean to give offense, yet my wretched shyness often makes me seem indifferent when I am merely awkward. Sometimes I think nature meant me for humbler company—I am so ill at ease among those of refinement.”

“Marianne cannot claim shyness as an excuse,” Elinor remarked.

“No,” Edward agreed. “She knows her own worth too well for false modesty.”

“Shyness,” he added after a moment, “is only the mark of feeling oneself inferior in some way. If I could believe my manners truly graceful, I should not be shy.”

“But you would still be reserved,” Marianne said pointedly. “And that is worse.”

Edward stiffened. “Reserved? Am I reserved, Marianne?”

“Yes. Very.”

He colored slightly. “I do not take your meaning. How so? What would you have me say?”

Elinor, startled by his reaction, sought to lighten the mood. “Surely you know my sister well enough to understand her? She calls everyone reserved who does not speak as quickly or admire things as rapturously as she does.”

Edward fell silent. The weight of his earlier melancholy settled over him once more, and for a long while, he said nothing at all.
